item.title: Aspen in My Heart
item.dc:creator: yourdressage
item.description:
After a year & a half of rehab I was riding at the walk for 15 mins & trot for 5 mins, & she was sound. Dr McRae told me I needed to get serious about dressage.

The post Aspen in My Heart first appeared on YourDressage.
item.content:encoded:
Healing, Heartbreak, and the Four-Year Ride to Region 6 Championships

By Cynthia Johnson

In March of 2020, just prior to my 60th birthday, I brought a horse named Aspen home. Aspen was a 14-year-old Thoroughbred mare that had been the personal horse of a certified Parelli Natural Horsemanship Instructor. She was horse that I thought would help me achieve my natural horsemanship goals. Aspen had been heavily featured in the Parelli promotional and training materials, and had lived on the Parelli ranch in Colorado for a number of years. You could safely say Aspen was a “schoolmaster” for someone with very lofty goals in natural horsemanship groundwork, freestyle riding, and liberty. I had been a Parelli student for almost 20 years, so the opportunity to partner with a horse like Aspen seemed to me to be an amazing stroke of luck!

Her owner was very particular in choosing a partner for Aspen, and I spent three months visiting her barn, where she coached me through groundwork and riding activities before she finally decided that I would be the right fit for Aspen. She was open in explaining that Aspen was talented, but complicated, and had been a very challenging mare. She explained that Aspen had arthritis, so should not be jumped, and had been on pasture rest the previous year to heal from an abscess. I had a dream of learning basic dressage, and Aspen’s owner agreed that she would be a good candidate for that.

The country was shutting down over Covid, and I keep my horses at my home, so I had plenty of uninterrupted time to get to know Aspen. I was excited to learn all I could from her. I had literally spent years watching her on instructional videos, so I felt like I had won the lottery when she became my partner! However, with the country on lockdown, I was primarily on my own in getting to know this new horse. Her previous owner came over a few times to help with the transition, but she did not live close, so we were limited in how often those visits were.

I gave Aspen a few days to settle in with my daughter’s horse and our mini, and then I took her to the arena to try some groundwork and liberty. I remember being shocked at how closely she watched me, and how every tiny movement, breath, and shift of weight that I made meant something to her.

Looking back, I can now see that my body language was too intense, and she was so sensitive and highly trained that she felt like I was yelling at her! She would spin, and rear, and take off and start jumping barrels in the arena at liberty! I remember that first time I was so scared that I literally took off running back up to the house!

Within a few days I had developed a healthy respect for her sensitivity (and significant fear!). I knew that regardless of how well she was trained, we needed to go back to the beginning, and put in the hours building a language together. This horse was not going to let me skip any steps.

After a few months together, things had settled. Aspen and I were doing better in our groundwork, and I could ride her at a walk, trot, and canter… though I must say her canter was a bit terrifying. It was fast and uncomfortable, and sometimes included a buck or two!

I found a local dressage instructor who was willing to help Aspen and I. Within a few lessons she explained that she thought Aspen was in pain. She felt I should stop riding until I had answers.

Aspen had been examined by a veterinarian, who had found nothing wrong, so my instructor suggested I call Dr. Crystal McRae. Dr. McRae came out, watched Aspen, and noted that she was very mildly lame. She did an ultrasound exam, finding that Aspen had what appeared to be two left hind suspensory tears – one medial and one branch. In her opinion the tears were likely not new, but were chronic old injuries that had never fully healed. Crystal explained that Aspen had a long recovery ahead of her, and that we could not be sure if she ever would be rideable.

Over the next year, I did everything I could for Aspen: shockwave therapy, stem cell injections, Bemer blanket therapy, red light therapy, and cold soaking. I even took an equine massage course to try to help her relax.

Aspen spent six months on stall rest and handwalking. Gradually, she was permitted to move into a double stall, and eventually a small paddock. She began groundwork at the walk and then the trot, with equicore bands.

After ten months, Dr. McRae gave me the all clear to trailer her to the trails and handwalk next to my daughter, who was riding. After a full year, I was finally allowed to ride her for five minutes at the walk! That was a huge moment… I knew that at least I would be able to ride my horse at the walk.

After a year and a half of slow rehab, I was riding her at the walk for 15 minutes and trotting for 5 minutes. She was staying sound. It was at that point that Dr. McRae told me that I needed to get serious about dressage. “She will not stay sound if you continue to ride her the way you are. She must learn to lift her back, step under herself, bend, and relax.”

We began our study of basic healthy biomechanics with online coach Kristi Smith, of Linda Parelli’s “How to Talk Horse” program. I would take PIVO videos, and she would send them back with coaching on core engagement, relaxation, and bend. We enrolled in “The Sweet Spot of Biomechanics” with Karen Rohlf, which was extremely helpful. I spent hours pouring over my videos and trying to improve.

In the fall of 2022 I decided that if I were going to ride dressage, I may as well go to a schooling show. I had never even been to one and I had no idea how they worked. But on a 22 degree November morning, I loaded Aspen in the trailer and headed to what was then Donida Farm in Auburn, Washington to compete in the Introductory A and B classes.

By this time, I was 62 and Aspen was 17. I was absolutely terrified and felt sick to my stomach. It had been 48 years since my last horse show as a child in Montana, and I had no idea what I was doing! When we got there I had to ask where to ride, and how I knew when it was my turn. We managed to ride both tests, and I was stunned when they handed me ribbons! I felt like I had climbed Mount Everest!

Aspen and I continued attending schooling shows throughout the year. Some went well, and some were pretty scary. I remember I got bucked off in the warm up ring once that first year. We were starting to work on Intro C, and we were cantering more often. Aspen was continuing to buck, occasionally. Dr. McRae examined her again and found that she had mild kissing spines. Back to rehab work with the equicore bands for us.

About two years after beginning dressage training I asked Dr. McRae to check Aspen for ulcers. She had exhibited none of the typical symptoms, but was still bucking occasionally at the canter, even though we had addressed the kissing spines, and a few times she had bucked me off. I was now 63, and it just wasn’t safe for me to be riding a bucking horse. Dr. McRae agreed that we should scope her, and what we found was shocking.

Aspen had grade 4 actively bleeding ulcers. The blood was evident everywhere on the camera, and it was heartbreaking. This poor mare had been doing her best for me, despite being in terrible pain. At first I felt awful for not finding the ulcers sooner. But Dr. McRae reminded me that we had been addressing everything as we found it, one issue at a time. First the suspensory tears, then the kissing spines, and finally, the ulcers.

In 2023 Aspen earned third place among all Thoroughbreds competing nationally in dressage through the Thoroughbred Incentive Program (T.I.P). She was named the Champion of Introductory Level Riders in the western region, and was the national champion in the 6 Feet on the Ground in-hand competition in both 2023 and 2024.

Aspen was back-to-back Reserve Champion in 2024 and 2025 amongst all Thoroughbreds competing nationally in dressage through T.I.P. She was Reserve National Champion for the 2025 6 Feet on the Ground in-hand competition.

Aspen turned 20 in April of 2025, and we celebrated at a horse show at Bello Acres (formerly Donida Farm). Aspen’s Jockey Club registration had her listed as “unnamed.” I found that heartbreaking – no one had even bothered to name her! For her birthday, I gave her the Jockey Club registered name, “Aspen in My Heart.”

In the spring of 2025 Aspen and I entered our first recognized show at Bello Acres, competing at Training Level. I had the goal to try to qualify for the Great American/USDF Region 6 Dressage Championships, but Aspen and I did not earn any qualifying scores that first year.

In the spring of 2026, I decided to try again, and we began working in-person with Kelly Irving-Burris. I still had my online coach, but I knew I needed more hands-on help. Kelly has been a perfect match for Aspen and I because she understands Aspen’s physical needs, her extreme sensitivity, and the importance of knowing when to stop. Aspen is a horse that will not tolerate being drilled on a skill.

As our partnership improved and Aspen’s core strength developed, we discovered a beautiful canter that I had never expected to find! Our scores improved as we became more supple and our tempo became consistent. In August, we received our second qualifying score! It had taken two years and18 rides to get those two scores… but we had done it!

This October we traveled to Great American/USDF Region 6 Championships at DevonWood Equestrian Centre in Oregon, with Kelly and her other students. When it came time to ride our championship test, I could not help myself. I was so overcome by the moment as I headed down centerline that tears rolled down my face and I began to cry. All I could think about was how very hard we had worked for this moment, and I wanted to enjoy and soak in every second of it with Aspen. I felt so blessed. That ride was truly in the top five moments of my life. I cried happy tears every stride, and was still crying for our final salute! We rode our personal best, placing fifth overall – more that I had even hoped for. Later that day, Aspen and I got to ride in the Parade of Champions!

About a year ago I researched Aspen’s Jockey Club history. I learned that she had been sent to auction as a yearling in Washington, failing to sell for $1400.00. She never recorded an official workout, and therefore was unraced. When I shared that with Joseph DiPietro, owner of Bello Acres and DiPietro Thoroughbreds, he explained that Aspen’s racing bloodlines are very strong, and the most likely reason a horse like that would not be entered into even one race would be because she got injured.

I have no way of knowing for certain if that was the case, but I do know that she is the maternal granddaughter of the legendary Sham, who finished second to Secretariat in the 1973 Kentucky Derby and Preakness Stakes. Her sire, Makors Mark, had a 29-race career, spanning five years. Aspen was clearly bred to race, so it is the most likely scenario that she was injured as a youngster, and has struggled with chronic pain and injuries most of her life.

When I think of Aspen, my heart is overwhelmed at what she has willingly done for her human partners. Her life has been spent helping humans achieve their personal goals. Her previous owner had her for eight years, during which Aspen helped her achieve her Level 4 in Parelli, and earn her Instructor’s Status. That is a very involved process for horse and rider, and takes years to accomplish. She participated in Parelli training videos which have been distributed around the world, and are used by students as they work to achieve their horsemanship goals with their own horses.

Now, Aspen has willingly partnered with me as I work to learn the art of dressage, and to rediscover the fun of competition, which was previously just a happy memory from my childhood in Montana, so many years ago.

Aspen and I are aging together; I am almost 66 and she is almost 22. I like to think we are keeping each other young, and I do my best each day to be the partner she deserves. I do still have dressage goals: I would love to return to Region 6 championships and compete at First Level, and it would be amazing if one day Aspen and I could enjoy our Century Ride together.

However, whether or not that happens, Aspen is in my heart, and we will only do what she is happy and willing to do. I truly feel that every ride with Aspen is a gift. However, riding is only one part of our story. If Aspen is ever uncomfortable under saddle, we will dedicate ourselves to our groundwork and liberty work, an area where Aspen is incredibly talented and truly thrives.

The post Aspen in My Heart first appeared on YourDressage.

item.title: Recognizing Youth Excellence: 2026 USDF/Dressage4Kids U-13 Regional Merit Awards
item.dc:creator: yourdressage
item.description:
The USDF/Dressage4Kids U-13 Regional Merit Awards recognize the two highest scoring 13-&-under riders at Training & First Levels at each Regional Championship.

The post Recognizing Youth Excellence: 2026 USDF/Dressage4Kids U-13 Regional Merit Awards first appeared on YourDressage.
item.content:encoded:
This year, a new award was presented at the 2026 Great American/USDF Regional Championships to honor a very special demographic in our community. With the generous support of Dressage4Kids, the brand new USDF/Dressage4Kids U-13 Regional Merit Awards recognize the highest and second highest placing 13-and-under riders in the Training and First Level Junior/Young Rider Championship classes at each of the nine Regional Championships.

In the press release announcing this new award and partnership, Lendon Gray – Olympian, USDF Hall of Famer, and Dressage4Kids founder – said it best: “We want to support the efforts of our youngest competitors and are delighted to recognize the hard work that these kids, and their wonderful instructors and parents, have done to get to their regional championships. We know they’ll be role models for others who are working for similar goals.”

As the 2026 Great American/USDF Regional Dressage Championships have now concluded, please join us in congratulating the winners from each region.

Region 1

2nd: Samantha Wood (13) & Rumor Has It

For over 25 years, Dressage4Kids has been committed to building a strong and sustainable future for the sport. Its mission remains the same today as it has always been: to encourage riders under 25 to become true horse people; to offer scholarships; to develop good sportsmanship; to support programs for adults who in turn educate youth, and to have fun! For more information on Dressage4Kids and their other programs and opportunities, visit the Dressage4Kids website.

For more information on the USDF/Dressage4Kids U-13 Regional Merit Awards, Great American/USDF Regional Championships, or other USDF youth opportunities and offerings, please visit the USDF website or contact regchamps@usdf.org.

item.title: Eleven Reigning Champions To Contest 2026 US Dressage Finals
item.dc:creator: yourdressage
item.category: US Dressage Finals Presented by Adequan
item.description:
By Alice Collins: No fewer than 11 of the 2025 champions are expected to return to the 2026 competition — some to defend their titles, others to campaign at new levels.

The post Eleven Reigning Champions To Contest 2026 US Dressage Finals first appeared on YourDressage.
item.content:encoded:
By Alice Collins 

The 13th running of the US Dressage (USDF) Finals presented by Adequan® will be held October 29 through November 1, 2026. For the second consecutive year, World Equestrian Center (WEC) in Wilmington, OH, will host the major national championship for juniors/young riders, adult amateurs (AA), and open riders, with classes from Training Level through Grand Prix and more than $125,000 in prize money.  

No fewer than 11 of the 2025 champions are expected to return to the 2026 competition — some to defend their titles, others to campaign at new levels. The premier event attracts competitors from every corner of the country, all aiming to capture the sashes, ribbons, and titles on offer. Championship classes, which are livestreamed on USEF Network via ClipMyHorse, are all held in climate-controlled arenas, and horses are housed in WEC – Wilmington’s more than 750 permanent climate-controlled stalls, minimizing disruptions from unpredictable fall weather in the region.  

Winner’s circle regular Heather Mason, from Lebanon, NJ, returns to the show with her 2025 open champions, Manuskript SCF and Rock It P. Manuskript SCF, a nine-year-old by Jazz x Krack C, is entered in three small tour classes this year, including two in which he will defend his titles. Rock It P (by Grand Galaxy Win x Everdale) was a double First Level champion in 2025 and will step up to compete in the straight and freestyle championships at Second Level.  

Mason always brings a large group of students and clients to Finals, and this year is no exception: she will be helping 20 riders with 30 horses — 10 amateurs and 10 professionals.  

“I’m very happy to be going back to WEC – Wilmington for Finals,” said Mason. “It’s such a great show to end the year with and offers great exposure and learning experiences for the horses. I decided to leave my other horses Sagacious P and Zhowie at home, even though they were qualified too, so I can have more time to coach my clients.” 

Among those clients is returning champion Emily O’Neill, who rode MW Empire to the Second Level Open title in 2025 and now returns at Third Level. Another of Mason’s clients is the prolific Adult Amateur Christina Morin-Graham, who earned three big tour titles with her two mares DSP Dauphin and Mondlicht in 2025. The rider from Malvern, PA, has again qualified both the Damon Hill daughter DSP Dauphin and her Sarkozy mare Mondlicht, with the latter entered in all three AA big tour classes.  

However, Morin-Graham does not plan to measure her success by the ribbon color.   

“I’m always just grateful to have horses who are fit and well,” she explained. “I don’t put too much pressure on myself; I’m just happy to be there and want to be a better rider for my horses. I focus less on my scores and defending my titles and more on actually improving. I have a growth mindset, and I’m more competitive with myself than with anyone else. So if I don’t defend my titles but ride better than last year, that’s a win for me.” 

Morin-Graham praised the climate-controlled facilities at WEC – Wilmington, adding: “The new venue for the Finals is fantastic. As a middle-aged rider with poor circulation, it was almost not viable for me to compete outside in November. We had a great time last year, so kudos to USDF for the shift that helps both horses and riders. Heather always brings so many people to Finals, and she’s so committed and gets everyone prepped. She’s outstanding, with so much wisdom and experience to offer.”   

Sarah Pyne’s remarkable story with her former three-star eventer Dirhon C is still being written. The 14-year-old gelding switched to dressage after falling very ill with EHV-5 — the equine herpes virus — four years ago, which permanently reduced his lung capacity. In 2025, the Diarado son surpassed all Pyne’s expectations, taking home the winner’s sash in the Fourth Level Freestyle AA championship. This year, they will leap up to Intermediate I level, which Pyne admits is a tall order.   

“Last year we were pretty dialed in at that level, and I knew we could be competitive,” she explained. “We’re not coming back in quite the same competitive fashion because we just moved up to the I1, so we’re still figuring the test out. This year’s aim is a solid test in front of a panel of high-quality judges.  

“It’s been so much fun to learn, grow, and move up the levels with Dirhon,” continued Pyne, a residential architect. “My trainer, Susanne Hamilton, wants him to go as high as he can, but I’ve been really putting her through the wringer. Not only have I moved, so all the training is online with Pivo, but she has to teach both him and me everything for every level since neither of us has done these movements before.” 

Since transitioning to dressage, Pyne has become an evangelist for the discipline, persuading numerous friends to make the switch. 

“I’m picking up my cousin Kathryn Schick on the way this year,” she said. “I convinced her to try dressage with her ex-upper-level eventer, and this is her first Finals. I told another friend with a barrel-racing background to try dressage. There have been others, too — all with horses that failed out of their original careers, but with owners who love them. Dressage is a great place for them to land career-wise.”  

Lauren Chumley and her distinctive 10-year-old mare, Leeloo Dallas, whom she bought unseen as a foal from Arizona breeder Racheal McKinney, were the Intermediate II Open champions in 2025 and will return to the Finals at the show’s highest level. 

“I’m excited to bring her back even though she’s super green at the level — this will be the fourth grand prix of her career, so I don’t have crazy expectations,” said Chumley, who is competing six of the nine horses traveling from her barn in Pittstown, NJ, to the Finals, including Leeloo Dallas’ four-year-old half-brother — out of the same Negro dam and by Lord Leatherdale — at Training Level.  

“I’m thrilled Leeloo has come this far at her age and is super happy in the work,” she continued. “It’s awesome to ride in that gorgeous arena in front of great judges. I love going to Finals; all my friends will be there, and that’s always fun.” 

Chumley’s entourage includes her trainer, Michael Bragdell, who is also competing, and her student, Mila Perry, who won two AA classes on the Jameson RS2 mare Jabberwocky Eden in 2025. Chumley helped Perry find Jabberwocky Eden as a three-year-old, and the pair have qualified for this year’s Finals in four classes.  

The 14-year-old rider Grace Christianson has also climbed the competition ladder with Outsider DRH. In 2025, she rode the then six-year-old Spielberg gelding to the Training Level Jr/YR title. This year, the duo returns to contend in the Third Level Jr/YR class and the Open Third Level Freestyle. Cody Armstrong Pierce and the six-year-old Floriscount mare Rhapsofloria have made an equally impressive leap up the levels. The 2025 Open Training Level champions will contest the Third Level championship in 2026.  

Returning 2025 champion combinations: 

  • 2025 Training Open champions Cody Armstrong Pierce and Rhapsofloria are entered in Third Level Open in 2026 
  • 2025 Second Open champions Nora Batchelder and Gnomonic are entered in Third Level Open, Fourth Level Open, and Fourth Level Open Freestyle  
  • 2025 Training Jr/YR champions Grace Christianson and Outsider DRH are entered in Third Level Jr/YR and Third Level Open Freestyle 
  • 2025 Intermediate II Open champions Lauren Chumley and Leeloo Dallas are entered in Grand Prix Open and Grand Prix Open Freestyle 
  • 2025 Prix St. Georges Open and Intermediate I Open Freestyle champions Heather Mason and Manuskript SCF are entered in Prix St. Georges Open, Intermediate I Open, and Intermediate Open Freestyle. 2025 First Level Open and First Level Open Freestyle champions Mason and Rock It P are entered in Second Level Open and Second Level Open Freestyle 
  • 2025 Grand Prix AA and Grand Prix AA Freestyle champions Christina Morin-Graham and DSP Dauphin are entered in Grand Prix AA and Grand Prix AA Freestyle. 2025 Intermediate II AA champions Morin-Graham on Mondlicht are entered in Intermediate II AA, Grand Prix AA, and Grand Prix AA Freestyle 
  • 2025 Second Level Freestyle Open champions Emily O’Neill and MW Empire are entered in Third Level Freestyle Open 
  • 2025 Training Level AA and First Level AA champions Mila Perry and Jabberwocky Eden are entered in First Level AA, First Level AA Freestyle, Second Level AA, and Second Level AA Freestyle
  • 2025 Fourth Level Open Freestyle champions Kymberly Pullen and Mojito are entered in Intermediate I Open Freestyle 
  • 2025 Fourth Level AA Freestyle champions Sarah Pyne on Dirhon C are entered in Intermediate I AA 
  • 2025 First Level Jr/YR and Second Level Jr/YR champions Autumn Vavrick on One De La Fazenda are entered in Third Level Jr/YR and Third Level Open Freestyle 

Riders competing at the 2026 US Dressage Finals presented by Adequan® qualified through nine Great American Insurance Group/USDF Regional Dressage Championships held in late September and early October. The 2026 Finals implemented a new, simplified entry process, eliminating the declaration and nomination processes. The top four eligible horse/rider combinations were automatically invited, and many minimum scores to earn a wildcard were reduced. See theUS Dressage Finals Eligibility Documentfor more information. 

A United States Equestrian Federation (USEF)-rated competition — the USDF Fall Classic — runs alongside the US Dressage Finals. It is open to both Finals and non-Finals horses, allowing competitors to bring additional horses to take advantage of WEC – Wilmington’s outstanding facilities.  

Alongside its top-level competitions, the 2026 US Dressage Finals offers a wide selection of shopping opportunities from an array of vendors, giving spectators the ideal opportunity to restock their favorite equestrian items, browse the latest styles, or pick up holiday gifts.   

For those who cannot attend, the Finals will be livestreamed on USEF Network via ClipMyHorse. Follow along via theUSDF Facebook page, USDF Instagram page. Full results can be found on HorseShowOffice.com. Along with presenting sponsor Adequan®, the 2026 US Dressage Finals is supported by SmartEquine and Platinum Performance. Contributing sponsors includePremier Equestrian, Sterling Thompson Equine, Schneiders, and Nutrena.   

Learn more by visiting the US Dressage Finals website. 

The post Eleven Reigning Champions To Contest 2026 US Dressage Finals first appeared on YourDressage.

item.title: My First Regional Championships with Mega
item.dc:creator: yourdressage
item.description:
"We competed in our very first dressage show in June, and since then I have completely fallen in love with the sport. I couldn't ask for a better partner."

The post My First Regional Championships with Mega first appeared on YourDressage.
item.content:encoded:
By Sierra Smoot

In September, my horse Mega and I made the trip to the Murieta Equestrian Center in Rancho Murieta for the 2026 Great American Insurance Group/USDF Region 7 Dressage Championships, held together with the California Dressage Society (CDS) State Championship. It was the biggest horse show I had ever been to, and what an amazing weekend it turned out to be!

Over four days of competition, we came home with three titles: USDF Region 7 Junior/Young Rider (Jr/YR) Training Level Champion, CDS Training Level Jr/YR Champion, and the very first USDF/Dressage4Kids U-13 Regional Merit Award, given to the highest-scoring rider aged 13 and under in the Training Level Jr/YR Championship. This is the first year USDF and Dressage4Kids have offered this award, which makes it even more special to me. Our regionals results also earned Mega and me the opportunity to compete at the US Dressage Finals!

Mega is my family’s horse. We imported him from Germany almost two years ago, originally to be a vaulting horse, but he has turned out to be so much more. He’s a gentle giant who loves attention and always wants someone scratching him or just touching him. He can be a little nervous when other horses come running toward him, and he has the loudest, most unmistakable whinny whenever his hauling buddy leaves him alone! But when I’m riding him, he always takes care of me and tries his hardest to do everything I ask. We competed in our very first dressage show in June, and since then I have completely fallen in love with the sport. I couldn’t ask for a better partner, and I’m so proud of how far we have come in such a short time.

Saturday night at the riders’ celebration dinner, I also got to participate in a vaulting demonstration with my club, Pacific Coast Vaulting, fresh from a sixth-place finish at the World Championships in Aachen. It felt like all my horse worlds showed up in one weekend!

Another thing that made this championship different from my other shows this summer was the people. At most of my other competitions, almost all the riders were adults, and I was usually one of the only kids. The funny thing is, I kept running into the same adults at each show, and I really enjoyed getting to know them. They love that I’m the young girl on the giant horse, and honestly, Mega is pretty hard to miss!

At the regional championships, there were youth riders from all over the region, and I got to know so many of them. Between our rides, we watched each other’s tests, cheered each other on, and traded stories about our horses. It was so nice to meet people my own age who love the same thing I love. By the end of the weekend, I felt like I had friends of every age cheering for me, and that I really belonged. I hope I get to see all of them at shows again next year.

Of course, none of this happens alone. A huge thank you to my coach, Carolyn Bland, who has always been there for me and is the reason I love dressage so much. I am so lucky to have her as my trainer! Thank you also to Terri Miller of Terri Miller Photos, who captured so many special moments from the championships, and to USDF and Dressage4Kids for creating an award that celebrates the youngest riders. I am so proud to be its first recipient in Region 7.

As for what’s next, Mega and I are moving up to First Level! The tests are longer, and the movements are harder, so we have a lot to practice this winter. I can’t wait to see what we can accomplish together.

More than anything, I’m proud of Mega. Less than four months ago, neither of us had ever competed in a dressage show, and now we’re regional champions! I never imagined that the horse we brought home from Germany for vaulting would take me on this amazing dressage adventure. I can’t wait to see where we go next!

The post My First Regional Championships with Mega first appeared on YourDressage.

item.title: A Full-Circle Journey to Gold
item.dc:creator: yourdressage
item.description:
Earning my Gold Medal was an incredible milestone, but the medal itself is only one part of the story. What matters more is everything it represents.

The post A Full-Circle Journey to Gold first appeared on YourDressage.
item.content:encoded:
By Kenzie Riddell

There was a time when I thought I might never ride seriously again.

In high school, I suffered a significant back injury that left me questioning whether riding would continue to have a place in my life. Horses have always been central to who I am. But, after breaking my back, the physical and emotional uncertainty that followed made stepping away feel like a real possibility.

College eventually brought me back to the sport through a very special horse named Oodles and trainer Holly Bergay.

Oodles gave me back something I was not sure I would ever fully regain: confidence, ambition, and the joy of working toward difficult goals in the saddle. Together, we progressed all the way to Prix St. Georges. She is an incredible horse and one of the most important partners I have ever had. I also knew that Prix St. Georges was likely where her competitive journey through the levels would end.

For a long time, I was content with that.

Then, I traveled with my younger sister, Kali Riddell, to the FEI North American Youth Championships and watched the Grand Prix class. Sitting there, watching those combinations enter the arena, I felt something shift. Grand Prix had always seemed like a distant goal—something I admired but was not sure I would ever personally experience. That weekend, though, the dream began to feel just close enough to reach.

When I returned home, I contacted a longtime friend from Arizona, Susan Skripac. Susan owned Wallace, an experienced Grand Prix horse, and I asked if she might allow me the opportunity to try the Grand Prix on him.

To say our first few rides were humbling would be an understatement.

I could not reliably ask for a clean flying change. I struggled to understand the contact he wanted. Wallace knew far more than I did, and in those early rides, I often felt as though we were speaking completely different languages. There were moments when I genuinely wondered whether this partnership was going to work at all.

I began riding Wallace in January 2026, and that was when Taylor McAnally became an essential part of the story.

Taylor’s skill as both a rider and a coach gave me the tools to begin understanding the somewhat nontraditional ride that is Wallace G. She helped me learn how to ride the horse underneath me rather than simply ask for movements I knew he could perform. With her guidance, the pieces slowly began to come together. Our changes became more consistent, contact began to make sense, and what had initially felt overwhelming gradually became possible.

At the same time, I was balancing this journey with life as a full-time law student at the Sandra Day O’Connor College of Law at Arizona State University. My days were spent moving between classes, legal research, assignments, and the barn. I was trying to give each responsibility the attention it deserved. It was not always easy, but riding Wallace became one of the most meaningful parts of that season of my life.

In March 2026, just a few months after first sitting on him, I competed at Intermediate II for the first time.

Then, in May, we traveled to Flintridge, where I rode my first-ever Grand Prix test.

Even writing that still feels surreal.

By early June, Wallace and I had earned the final scores needed for my USDF Gold Medal.

The moment itself carried an unexpected sense of symmetry. The final Grand Prix test that gave me the score I needed was judged by the same judge who had judged my very first leadline class years earlier. It happened to be at the very same show facility as well.

There was something almost impossible to put into words about realizing how much had happened between those two rides.

From a little girl being led around an arena, to a high school student wondering whether a broken back might end her time in the saddle, to a college rider rediscovering the sport through Oodles, and finally to riding down centerline at Grand Prix. It felt like the kind of full-circle moment you cannot plan.

More than anything, though, this accomplishment belongs to the people and horses who made it possible.

I will always be grateful to Oodles for bringing me back to riding and carrying me farther than I once thought I would go. And I am eternally grateful to Susan and Taylor for giving me an opportunity that changed my life.

Susan’s generosity in trusting me with Wallace is something I will never take for granted. Grand Prix horses are extraordinary teachers, but access to a horse like Wallace is never something to which anyone is entitled. Susan gave me the chance to learn from him, make mistakes, grow, and experience a level of the sport I had dreamed about for years.

Taylor, meanwhile, gave me the knowledge and confidence to make that opportunity meaningful. Her patience, talent, and ability to communicate what Wallace needed helped transform a partnership that initially felt uncertain into one that allowed me to achieve one of my greatest riding goals.

Neither of them had to give me what they did. They made a choice.

That generosity and kindness are what I will remember most. Their generosity also taught me something larger about the sport of dressage. I was not able to reach Grand Prix because I suddenly had all the answers, but because two people were willing to open a door for me. Susan trusted me with an extraordinary horse, and Taylor invested her time, knowledge, and patience into teaching me how to ride him well. That kind of generosity creates opportunities that can completely change a rider’s path.

Dressage is a sport that takes years to learn, and progressing through the upper levels requires access not only to talented horses, but also to experienced trainers and mentors who are willing to share what they know. I was incredibly fortunate to have both. My experience with Wallace showed me how powerful it can be when accomplished horsewomen help create a pathway for another rider to learn, make mistakes, grow, and ultimately rise through the levels.

I hope our sport continues to encourage more of that. There are talented, hardworking riders who may never have the opportunity to experience the upper levels simply because they have not yet had access to the right horse, instruction, or mentorship. When owners, trainers, and experienced riders are willing and able to share opportunities, they do more than help someone earn a score or a medal—they help develop the next generation of dressage riders.

I will always be grateful that Susan and Taylor did that for me. Their generosity gave me the opportunity to accomplish a dream I once thought might remain forever out of reach, and it showed me firsthand just how meaningful it can be when someone in this sport reaches back and helps another rider succeed.

Earning my Gold Medal was an incredible milestone, but the medal itself is only one part of the story. What matters more is everything it represents: returning to a sport I once thought I might lose, trusting the process when things felt difficult, finding people willing to believe in me, and being reminded that sometimes the opportunities that change our lives begin simply by being brave enough to ask.

Wallace gave me the chance to ride Grand Prix.

Susan and Taylor gave me the chance to believe I belonged there.

And for that, I will be grateful for the rest of my life.

The post A Full-Circle Journey to Gold first appeared on YourDressage.

item.title: Mules Can Do Dressage!
item.dc:creator: yourdressage
item.description:
By Amber Heintzberger: Originally bred as pack animals, mules make a unique addition to the dressage scene

The post Mules Can Do Dressage! first appeared on YourDressage.
item.content:encoded:
Originally bred as pack animals, mules make a unique addition to the dressage scene

With their long ears and unique conformation, mules don’t exactly blend in at dressage shows. Although they’re typically associated with pulling wagons or mountain pack trips, mules can and do compete in dressage!

When we checked, a total of 60 mules were registered with the USDF to compete in licensed dressage competition. Of those, 44 have competed at least once in the past two years—a few at the FEI levels. Let’s meet a few of these successful dressage longears and their human partners.

Buckeye: The Model Mule

Fans of Breyer model horses may remember Buckeye, a leopard Appaloosa mule owned by Christina Gregory and ridden by Samantha Majors, who competed in both traditional (at First and Second Levels) and Western dressage. Buckeye was immortalized as a Breyer, and he and Majors appeared at Breyer’s annual collectors extravaganza, Breyerfest, at the Kentucky Horse Park in 2019.

Now being ridden by Majors’ mom, Jenni, Buckeye also competes in jumping. The eye-catching spotted equine made a repeat appearance at Breyerfest in 2025, to the delight of mule fans everywhere.

Tom Collins: Every Day Is Mule Day

Known for its annual Mule Days festival, Bishop, California has become synonymous with mules. Bishop native and professional horse trainer Rebecca Evans made a name for herself in the dressage world with a mule named Tom Collins.

Evans explains that a client had asked her to find “a dressage mule that could also go fox hunting.” She found Tom Collins in Oregon.

“I liked him because he was balanced and uphill, and had good suspension,” Evans says. “Mules tend to be pretty flat or have a more downhill build.” A good dressage horse has “swing” in its back, she explains, but “a mule doesn’t have the same lateral movement as a horse. By design, they are pulling animals and take the load on their forehand. They’re also very smart. So when you’re training for dressage and moving up the levels, you have to be pretty specific when you’re training them. Finding that balance can be difficult, but once they figure something out, they can replicate it. So you have to be astute as a trainer and also have a mule that can do that.”

Now based in Middleburg, Virginia, Evans was raised in Bishop, a central-California town near the Nevada border, where grew up riding and at age 14 began working for trainers. The husband of one trainer owned a pack station, and in their early twenties Evans and her twin sister began working for the station, which packed supplies (on mules, of course) into the Sierras for guests who were hiking and camping in the back country.

“Not long after that, a vet came to me about training a mule he wanted to compete in jumping and dressage at Mule Days,” Evans says. “It escalated from there.”

She calls Mule Days “a big thing” and notes with some bemusement that “in the horse world, a lot of trainers, the higher up you go, don’t have a lot of respect for mules.” She says she once asked a mule trainer whether he liked working with mules. “He was quiet for a bit and then said, ‘I like training mules because they make me a better horse trainer.’”

To train a mule successfully, Evans says, “you have to have infinite patience, a sense of humor, and you have to finesse it. They’re so smart, you can’t coerce them into anything. It’s hard! It’s not an easy job.”

In 2019, Evans and Tom Collins qualified to compete at the US Dressage Finals presented by Adequan®, where they finished ninth in the Second Level Open division.

“One of the judge’s comments was that the mule ‘does everything with a smile on his face,’” she recalls. “To have a judge really see that is something. You have to have a good working relationship with a mule or you’re never going to get them to do anything. It was really fun to be there, and of course people loved him. He had a little fan club after that!”

Evans remains a staunch advocate for mules in equestrian sport. “The amount of work put into them is the same for any other show horse, and they deserve just as much recognition,” she says.

Heart B Porter Creek: FEI Mule

At around age 12, Audrey Goldsmith saw her first mules while on a family vacation to the Grand Canyon and “thought, ‘I’m gonna have me one of those someday!’”

Years later, Goldsmith’s interest in mules was reignited after she attended Mule Days in California. Then a hunter/jumper trainer, she decided it would be fun to “explore different aspects of riding.” She purchased two mules, one of which was the three-day-old Heart B Porter Creek. (“I’d been in touch with the breeders, and I made a totally unprofessional decision and bought him sight unseen,” she confesses.)

With “Porter” and his half-brother, Tuxedo, Goldsmith has won numerous championships in disciplines ranging from jumping, English and Western pleasure, and trail to dressage. At first, dressage was more prescriptive than competitive for Porter, however.

“We lived in California not far from the ocean, and I’d take him to the beach and take him for walks,” she recalls. “But then he started tripping and falling on his knees, and I was fairly certain he was neurological, but it was much harder to get these things diagnosed then. A friend brought a young dressage horse over, and she suggested I try dressage with him to help with his back and his balance, and that was the beginning of the journey.”

In 2003, Goldsmith began campaigning Porter in licensed dressage competition. The pair successfully rose up the levels to Prix St. Georges; and Goldsmith earned her USDF bronze and silver medals aboard her mule—the first time a mule has earned that distinction.

Eventually, dressage with Porter became a passion project rather than a training tool.

“His scores were insane; he was just amazing,” Goldsmith says. She says that most dressage judges received the long-eared equine warmly (although “[the late] Colonel Burton just couldn’t cope with a mule!”) and that “a couple of competitors were disgruntled,” but the general public embraced Porter, who had a fan club and a Facebook page, she says.

After earning very respectable scores at Training and First Levels, “we really struggled in the deep, dark hole of Second Level, but everyone kept encouraging me,” Goldsmith says. Porter, she says, “was so obedient and had three good gaits. He was half-Thoroughbred, and even his canter was good. His changes were clean, though he always swung his hind end, but everything was accurate and he was so well-behaved. Sometimes I’ll look back and think it was just a gift, but I’ll look at videos and see that no, he really did earn it.”

Goldsmith, who’s now based in Oregon, tips her hat to fellow mule enthusiast Laura Hermanson of California, who with the molly mule Heart B Dyna became the first mule/rider pair to compete at the US Dressage Finals, in 2015. The following year, Hermanson returned to the Kentucky Horse Park for Finals with another mule, Behold the Desert.

Another of Goldsmith’s shout-outs goes to the well-known mule trainer Meredith Hodges, owner of Lucky Three Ranch in Colorado and daughter of the late legendary Peanuts cartoonist Charles M. Schulz. Hodges is “the person I went to, to help fund mules in the [Adequan®/USDF] All-Breeds Program…. Meredith sponsored ten years of All-Breeds for the American Mule Association,” she says.

Goldsmith is proud of what she’s accomplished on her mules, noting that she takes dressage competition seriously; for her, a mule is not a cute sideshow attraction amidst the warmbloods.

“One of the tests I saved, the comment was ‘seamless test,’” she says. “I should put it in a frame. That’s the goal. And to do it on a mule, that was awesome to me.”

Editor’s note: At press time, the American Mule Association was not an Adequan®/USDF All-Breeds participating organization. To learn more about mules, visit the American Mule Association’s website.

The post Mules Can Do Dressage! first appeared on YourDressage.

item.title: When One Door Closes
item.dc:creator: yourdressage
item.category: Great American Insurance Group/USDF Regional Championships
item.description:
If someone had told me that a phone call following one of the hardest days would lead me to another special Fjord, I probably wouldn't have believed them.

The post When One Door Closes first appeared on YourDressage.
item.content:encoded:
By Taylor Pelcher

Last month, we celebrated the feisty Norwegian Fjord as our Breed of the Month on YourDressage! Did you know that dressage riders who choose a registered Fjord as their dressage mount are eligible for special awards through the Adequan®/USDF All-Breeds Awards program? The Norwegian Fjord Horse Registry and the Norwegian Fjord Horse Alliance Inc. are participating organizations! 

Finding out that my Zangersheide, Caliber, had sustained a significant tear to his deep digital flexor tendon and would need to be retired was not what I had in my plan for September of 2024. But, as it turns out, the universe had other plans. I called a close friend to share the news, and the very next day she called me back with an idea. A good friend of hers had a young Fjord, Bear Creek’s Kirby, or Lars, who needed a job for the fall and winter.

I have had a Fjord in my life since 2008, so I already knew and loved the breed. What I wasn’t particularly looking for was another horse. I certainly wasn’t expecting a young Fjord to enter my life at that particular moment. But when I learned that Lars was very green (lightly started under saddle, both in the arena and on the trail), I was intrigued. I gave it about an hour of thought and agreed to pick him up in mid-October. Long story short, I ended up with a six-month trial on Lars, with the opportunity to purchase him at the end if I decided he was a good fit.

Looking back, it really was the definition of kismet. Caliber needed to retire, and Lars needed a job.

Our first winter together was all about getting to know each other. Lars was four, with a busy little mind and plenty to learn. We trail rode through the snow, found ways to keep him occupied, and generally spent a lot of time figuring each other out. He was sensible, brave, curious, and he had a way of making me smile. All. The. Time.

By the time I reached the halfway point of our time together, the decision to buy him wasn’t particularly difficult. His personality was like none other, and I had become completely attached to this sweet boy. I had no idea exactly where our partnership would take us, but I knew I wanted to find out.

When spring arrived, we were able to start building on everything we’d done over the winter. My goal for that first summer was exposure and experience; Lars needed mileage. We went on as many field trips as possible. We took lessons, attended clinics, went trail riding, participated in a hunter pace, and went to a schooling show. In August, we wrapped up the summer with a recognized show, where we competed in the Introductory Opportunity classes. It was a wonderful experience and gave me a true glimpse of what Lars might be capable of.

I knew that Lars had real athletic potential in him. I was excited to see what we could do with some more focused training and began making plans to dive into a more structured training program with our amazing trainer, Kimberley Omans, and see what the winter would bring.

As it turns out, it brought a lot.

2026 has been an incredible year for us. Lars turned six this summer, and he has stepped up to the plate every time I’ve asked him to. We made our Training Level debut, earned the scores we needed to qualify for the Great American/USDF Regional Dressage Championships, and then went on to qualify at First Level as well. We recently wrapped up our season at the USDF Region 8 Championships, where Lars put in three solid tests between Training and First Level. To watch this little Fjord walk into a Regional Championship arena and hold his own among some very fancy dressage horses was pretty special. 

Lars has taught me to appreciate the process. When I first brought him home, I wasn’t thinking about horse showing at all. I was thinking about giving a young horse a job, keeping his mind busy, and seeing what kind of partnership we could build. Everything else has come one step at a time.

Already having a Fjord, Lars reinforced the way I think about dressage horses. I have always loved dressage, and I’ve ridden and worked with many different types of horses over the years, but Lars has reminded me that a dressage horse doesn’t have to fit a particular mold. He may be a little shorter, a little hairier, and considerably more compact than the horses he often shares the warm-up ring with, but he is every bit as much a dressage horse. He is athletic, willing, incredibly brave, and always trying to figure out what I’m asking. And he has a personality that makes every ride an adventure.

Some of my favorite moments with Lars actually have nothing to do with dressage. I love taking him out on the trail, introducing him to new things, and watching him experience something for the first time. Those early field trips were such an important part of building his confidence, and I still love getting him out of the arena. He is the kind of horse who makes even the ordinary days at the barn fun.

I’m incredibly grateful for the people who have helped us along the way, especially my special friend Carol, who connected me with Lars in the first place. It truly is about timing and who you know! Kimberley has been such an important part of our journey, helping us develop Lars’s potential and keep raising the bar. I’ve also been fortunate to learn from wonderful clinicians, including, but not limited to, Felicitas von Neumann-Cosel, JJ Tate, and Gary Rockwell, and to have so many friends and family cheering us on. Team Lars keeps growing, and we are so appreciative of everyone who has become part of our journey.

Looking ahead, we’re not planning to slow down. We’ll continue training throughout the fall and winter, using the off-season to build strength, balance, and confidence. Our plan for 2027 is to keep building on what we’ve accomplished, qualify for First Level again, and hopefully give Second Level a try. I’m excited to see how Lars develops over the winter and where he tells us he’s ready to go next. I don’t feel the need to rush him. For now, I’m excited to keep learning, keep improving, and see just how far this little Fjord can go.

If our story encourages even one person to take a second look at the Fjord breed as a potential dressage partner, I’ll consider that a pretty great thing. I would absolutely encourage anyone looking for a dressage partner not to overlook a Fjord simply because they don’t fit the traditional picture of a dressage horse. They are smart, willing, athletic, and incredibly versatile, and, in my experience, they bring a whole lot of personality to the partnership, too.

If someone had told me in September of 2024 that a phone call following one of the hardest days would lead me to another special Fjord, I probably wouldn’t have believed them. I didn’t know just how much this particular Fjord would come to mean to me. Sometimes the best partnerships aren’t the ones you plan. Sometimes they are the ones that find you.

I am incredibly proud of Lars, beyond grateful for the journey we’ve had so far, and very excited to see what comes next.

The post When One Door Closes first appeared on YourDressage.

item.title: Beyond The Saddle
item.dc:creator: yourdressage
item.description:
In 2024 I graduated from Rutgers University with a BA in English Literature. Unsure of what I wanted to do next, I decided to take a year off to figure it out.

The post Beyond The Saddle first appeared on YourDressage.
item.content:encoded:
Keeping Horses In Your Life Through The Different Seasons

By Nicole Sofocli

In the span of a year and a half, I went from riding up to five times a week, to once a week, then once a month. My riding schedule has varied throughout the different seasons of my life, but I’ve always found a way to keep horses as a constant in my life, even if it meant riding less frequently.

From ages twelve to sixteen, I was a once-a-week lesson kid. Some summers, I attended horse camp, but my riding schedule was always dependent on my parents’ ability to take me to the barn. 

When I turned seventeen and got my driver’s license, I began half-leasing a horse. My lease ended in the midst of COVID, and after I graduated from high school, I left the barn and stopped riding for almost a year. It was the longest I had gone without riding since I started taking lessons.

Towards the end of my freshman year of college, which was online, I wanted to ride again. So, I got a job at a local horse farm mucking stalls, feeding and watering the horses, and teaching some beginner lessons. That fall, when I was able to attend college in person, I joined the Rutgers University Dressage Team. Over winter break, I became a working student for the Rutgers dressage coach. I worked and rode there for the next three years of my college career.

In 2024, after changing my major three times, I graduated from Rutgers University with a bachelor’s degree in English Literature. Unsure of what I wanted to do next, I decided to take a year off to figure it out.

Outside of a month of travel, my only plans for the summer were to ride, work at the farm, and have fun. Knowing that I thrive on a consistent schedule and routine, I set some parameters for myself during my gap year: I would give myself the summer to enjoy some time off and recover from the burnout of school; then, come September, I would come up with a plan for when my gap year was over.

When I came back from traveling at the beginning of August, I spent as much time as I could at the farm. I was there anywhere from three to five days per week. My trainer would let me work off my lessons, so I would spend the entire day at the farm working and riding.

I had made an extensive list of things I wanted to accomplish over the year. The list was ambitious, and my plan was never to accomplish everything, but as I thought of things that I had always wanted to do, big or small, I added them to the list: learn Greek, take a road trip to D.C., learn how to style my natural curls. Of the eighteen items on the list, four centered around horses: showing First Level, learning to drive a horse trailer, improving my physical health to better my riding, and starting a riding journal. 

From August to October, I showed First Level, learned to drive a trailer, started taking barre classes, and kept a running list of notes from my lessons. Horses consumed all of my time in one way or another throughout those three months. Not only was I spending extensive time at the barn, but when I wasn’t there, I was actively doing things to improve my riding. 

I would watch videos of my lessons and jot down notes – just little things, a few words of a metaphor or analogy that my trainer used to explain different concepts to me, or a couple of buzz words that would remind me of things to keep in mind that we worked on during the previous lesson. Things like “water bucket”; my trainer would say, “Imagine the feeling of holding out a water bucket in your outside hand with the rein” to illustrate the feeling of outside rein contact, to highlight what muscle the contact should come from. She then gave me a water bucket to hold while I rode to get that feeling. 

Keeping a riding journal was especially helpful when time grew longer between rides. Before my lesson, I could open my notes and remind myself what we had been previously working on. This allowed me to make the most of my limited riding time as I was able to pick up where we had left off more easily. 

During the months I was riding numerous times a week, I was also taking barre classes three to four times a week to improve my strength and balance. Barre quickly revealed the differences between my right and left sides, including which side I favored, which side was stronger, and where I have a tendency to lean. All things that showed up in my riding were made very apparent when taking the barre classes. 

For example, I became very aware of the strength imbalance between my right and left sides during seat work. During classes, I found that if my left leg was the supporting leg first, it would fatigue much more quickly than if I began by working my left side and then switched to the right. My right leg was noticeably less fatigued after being the supporting leg, the transition from supporting to working leg was much easier. This highlighted the fact that my left side was weaker than my right. 

As I continued taking barre classes and consistently strengthening both sides, the asymmetry in my riding began to even out. Staying consistent with the barre classes allowed me to retain muscle and keep my riding skills sharp so I could avoid regressing when I inevitably went longer than I’d like between rides. 

During my gap year, I volunteered at a Stephen Peters clinic, audited Ingrid Klimke’s Masterclass at Dressage at Devon, attended Rutgers Intercollegiate Dressage Association (IDA) shows, and, when I wasn’t riding at the barn, watched other people ride. When the chiropractor or the dentist was coming, my trainer would let me know so I could be there to observe. Watching the chiropractor work taught me about horse biomechanics and helped me better understand horses’ natural movements, and understanding the fundamental mechanics of a horse and why they respond a certain way, not just how they will respond to certain aids, helped the progression of my riding immensely. 

Summer came and went very quickly. When fall came around, I was consumed with graduate school applications and a graduate class that I was auditing at Rutgers. I went from being at the barn three to five days a week, to going once a week for a lesson on my way home. The transition from so much uninterrupted time to ride and learn at the barn to making less frequent trips made me even more appreciative of every moment spent there, whether riding or just observing.

During my gap year, I learned how to incorporate riding and related activities into every season of my life. I learned that the work done outside the saddle, both physical and educational, is just as important – and sometimes even more important – than the time spent riding. By continuing to work on my riding outside of the saddle, I could make the most of the limited time I had in it. I consumed everything horse-related around me and took every opportunity to learn. 

I went into my gap year knowing that I would probably never again have that kind of time to dedicate to my riding, so I soaked up every bit of time with horses that I could. The biggest takeaway from my gap year wasn’t the progression of my riding itself; it was about reframing my idea of what keeping horses in my life looks like. Just because I’m not physically able to get to the barn to ride doesn’t mean I’m not actively working towards my passion. I came out of my gap year with an understanding of how to nurture my passion for riding throughout the different seasons of my life and that there is no time limit for accomplishing my equestrian-related goals.
